# 1. POPULATION AND DEMOGRAPHICS

## 1.1 The 2024 national census — the anchor number

Iraq ran its first full census in 27 years on **20–22 November 2024** (the 10th in Iraqi history, and the first since 2003). Final results were announced by the Minister of Planning on **24 February 2025**.

| Metric | Value | Source / year |
|---|---|---|
| ★ Total population (incl. foreign residents) | **46,118,793** | Iraqi Ministry of Planning, final census results, Feb 2025 |
| Iraqi nationals only (excl. foreigners) | 45,778,662 | Same |
| Male / Female | 23.161M (50.2%) / 22.957M (49.8%) | Same |
| Urban / Rural | **70.17% / 29.83%** | Same |
| Households | 7,898,588 | Same |
| Average household size | 5.7 persons (census); 5.9 (IHSES 2023/24) | MoP census 2024; IHSES 2023/24 |
| Annual population growth rate | **2.3%** | MoP census 2024 |

**Why this matters for SHABM:** 2.3% annual growth on a 46M base = **~1.06 million new Iraqis per year**, i.e. a new city the size of Basra every 2 years. The addressable market is not static.

## 2.4 IQD / USD — official vs parallel (critical for the financial model)

**This is the single most important operational finance fact in this report.** Revenue is collected in IQD at street prices. Imported equipment (ultra-low-temperature freezers, rolled-ice-cream pans, ice-block machines, silicone fruit moulds), imported dairy, and imported coffee are paid for in USD — and unless you can access the CBI official window through a compliant bank, you buy dollars at the parallel rate. **Every USD cost line in the model should be stressed at 1,530, not 1,310.** A model built at 1,310 overstates USD-denominated gross margin by roughly 17%.

# 3. IRAQ / BAGHDAD CAFÉ AND RESTAURANT MARKET

## 3.1 Size of the branded / organised segment — the real competitive set

The gold-standard source here is **World Coffee Portal's Project Café Middle East 2025**:

| Metric | Value | Source / year |
|---|---|---|
| ★ **Iraq branded coffee shop outlets** | **85** | Project Café Middle East 2025, World Coffee Portal |
| Iraq's rank in MENA | **13th largest branded market** | Project Café Middle East 2025 |
| Iraq forecast | **>130 outlets by end-2029** (~10% growth) | Project Café Middle East 2025 |
| ★ MENA branded coffee shop market | **11,163 outlets**, **+11.2% y/y** | Project Café Middle East 2025 |
| MENA forecast | 12,160 outlets by Nov 2025; **16,460 by Nov 2029 (8.1% CAGR)** | Project Café Middle East 2025 |
| Saudi Arabia | **5,130 outlets = 46% of all MENA stores** | Project Café Middle East 2025 |
| Fastest-growing MENA markets by outlets | Morocco (+19%), Saudi (+16.5%), Egypt (+13.3%) | Project Café Middle East 2025 |

**This is the white-space slide.** Iraq has 46 million people and **85 branded coffee outlets** — one per ~542,000 people. Saudi Arabia has ~34 million people and 5,130 outlets — one per ~6,600 people. Iraq is under-penetrated versus Saudi by a factor of **~80×**. Even if you assume Iraq only ever reaches one-tenth of Saudi's density, that implies ~7,000 branded outlets — an 80× expansion from today.

## 3.2 Total restaurant count (the unorganised market)

| Metric | Value | Source / year |
|---|---|---|
| ★ Registered restaurants in Iraq | **23,718** (reported as ">24,000") | Iraqi Ministry of Planning, cited by Infoplus Network / Mustaqila, 2025–26 |
| Excludes | sidewalk, small, mobile, temporary, unregistered and "hidden" restaurants | Same |
| Restaurant/food-service share of Iraqi commercial establishments | **~65%** (as reported) | Ministry of Planning, cited by Infoplus, 2025–26 |
| Sector growth rate | **3–6% per year**, driven by youth demand, delivery apps, new local investment | Mustaqila (وكالة الصحافة المستقلة), 2026 |
| Registered restaurants in Baghdad | ">500" — **this figure is internally inconsistent** | Mustaqila, 2026 |

**Data-quality flag — important.** The Mustaqila article is literally headlined *"سوق المطاعم في بغداد.. أرقام متضاربة"* ("Baghdad's restaurant market: conflicting numbers"). It states 24,000 nationally but only ">500 in Baghdad alone" while simultaneously saying most restaurants are concentrated in Baghdad. Those cannot both be true. Treat ">500" as either a sub-category (e.g. licensed large/luxury restaurants) or an error.

> **ESTIMATE — Baghdad registered restaurant count:** Baghdad holds 21.2% of Iraq's population, is 85% urban, and has the country's lowest poverty rate outside Kurdistan, so its share of restaurants should exceed its population share. Applying a 25–35% share to 23,718 gives **≈5,900–8,300 registered restaurants in Baghdad Governorate**, plus a large unregistered tail. Confidence: low-medium — derived, not sourced.

> **ESTIMATE — modern/specialty cafés in Baghdad:** of Iraq's 85 branded outlets, Baghdad likely holds 55–70% given it is the largest market and home to the leader (Ridha Alwan) and the fastest-growing chain (The Grinders, 17 branches). That implies **≈47–60 genuinely branded/specialty café outlets in a city of 9.8 million** — roughly one per 165,000–210,000 residents. Confidence: medium.

## 3.3 Named operators — the real competitive map

**Domestic Iraqi:**
- ★ **Ridha Alwan Coffee (بن رضا علوان)** — founded **1960**, East Karrada. Explicitly named by World Coffee Portal as **the domestic market leader**. Evolved from a traditional cultural coffeehouse (poetry evenings, film festivals, intellectual gatherings) into a full retail coffee brand and roastery over the last decade. Also the institutional force behind the Baghdad Coffee & Tea Festival via the **Ridha Alwan Cultural Foundation**.
- ★ **The Grinders (@thegrinders.iq)** — launched **2020**; **13 branches** as of the 2024 Iraqi News round-up; **17th branch opened in Al-Ameriyah, Baghdad, March 2025**. Locations confirmed in Zayouna (Rubaie St), Jadriya, Yarmouk, Al-Ameriyah, "4 Streets", plus Diyala. Serves plant-based milks, juices and lemonade alongside espresso — i.e. **already competing on cold/non-coffee**.
- **Agora** — opened early 2024, rapidly became a youth favourite in Baghdad on "cozy/calm vibes."
- **Al-Reef Café** — Karrada, named one of Baghdad's best.
- **IN OFF Cafe** — Arasat Al-Hindiya; 345+ menu items across two floors, fine dining + specialty coffee + premium shisha. This is the format your Arasat competitor set looks like.
- **Al-Faisaliya Restaurant & Cafe** — modern upscale, explicitly "distinctive youthful décor."
- **Coffeella Cafe** — listed on Pulled.coffee as a Baghdad specialty shop.
- Heritage coffeehouses (context, not competition): **Shabandar Café** (1917, Al-Mutanabbi St), **Al-Zahawi Café** (1917, Al-Rashid St), **Al-Beiruti Café** (Tigris riverfront), **Dar al-Atraqchi**, **Brazilian Café**.

**Foreign brands already in Iraq:**
- **Espressolab** (Türkiye) — branch in central Baghdad.
- **Mikel Coffee** (Greece), **Caffè Vergnano 1882** (Italy) — named by World Coffee Portal as present in the Iraqi market.
- **Shaghf Coffee** (UAE), **Dose Cafe** (Kuwait) — Gulf operators in-market.
- ★ **Kyan Café** (Saudi Arabia) — opened its **first Iraq outlet in Basra as a drive-thru**; has publicly stated plans for **Baghdad, Karbala and Erbil**. Kyan's positioning is explicitly *"a heavily iced coffee menu"*. **This is your closest strategic analogue and your most direct future competitor.**
- ★ **Half Million** (Saudi Arabia) — announced first Iraq outlet for H2 2025, **debuting at Baghdad's Iraq Mall**; second Saudi coffee chain into the market.
- **Cinnabon** — first Iraq store opened **February 2023 in Al-Jadriya, Baghdad**.
- **Morelli's Gelato** — Baghdad outlet opened 2021, **near the main gate of the University of Baghdad (Jadriya)**.
- Fast food already present: Hardee's, Papa John's, Texas Chicken (Church's), Burger King (12 outlets nationally as of the Erbil third-outlet opening).

**Names in the brief I could NOT verify:** I ran targeted searches for **Kahvi, Karam (as a coffee brand), Turk Coffee, Loyal, Bab, and Mokha** as Baghdad coffee operators and found **no substantiating English or Arabic sources**. ("Karam Baghdad Restaurant" exists as an Iraqi-cuisine restaurant, not a coffee brand; "Mokkador" appears as a Coffee Festival exhibitor.) **Do not put these names on an investor slide without local verification** — an Iraqi investor will know instantly if the competitive map is wrong.

## 3.4 Prices in Baghdad — what a cup actually costs

| Item | IQD | USD | Source / year |
|---|---|---|---|
| ★ Cappuccino (regular, restaurant) | **3,300 IQD** | $2.20–2.60 | world-prices.com / hikersbay, Baghdad, **2026** |
| Cappuccino (Iraq national avg) | 2,900 IQD | $2.20 | hikersbay Iraq, 2026 |
| Espresso | 2,000 IQD | $1.60 | hikersbay Baghdad, 2026 |
| Latte | ~1,500–1,800 IQD | **$1.16** | Coffeestics Iraq (low-end/mass-market read) |
| Cold brew | ~2,200 IQD | $1.69 | Coffeestics Iraq |
| Mocha | ~2,650 IQD | $2.04 | Coffeestics Iraq |
| **Frappuccino / blended iced** | **~4,900 IQD** | **$3.78** | Coffeestics Iraq |
| McMeal (McDonald's/BK equivalent combo) | 8,000–9,700 IQD | $6.10–7.50 | hikersbay / world-prices Baghdad, 2026 |
| Cheeseburger | 2,400–2,900 IQD | $1.80–2.20 | hikersbay / world-prices Baghdad, 2026 |
| Coca-Cola 2L (retail) | 1,635 IQD | ~$1.25 | Expatistan Baghdad, 2026 |
| Three-course meal for two | ~48,000 IQD | ~$37 | hikersbay Baghdad, 2026 |
| Monthly cost, single person, ex-rent | — | ~€570 | Numbeo Baghdad, updated **10 July 2026** (650 entries, 37 contributors, past 12 months) |
| Family of four, monthly, ex-rent | — | ~€1,910 | Numbeo Baghdad, July 2026 |

Numbeo ranks Baghdad **1st cheapest of 41 Western Asian cities** for both "meal at an inexpensive restaurant" and "soft drinks." Dining out in Baghdad is **~55% cheaper than the United States** (world-prices, 2026).

> ★ **ESTIMATE — iced latte price in a modern Baghdad specialty café: 4,000–6,500 IQD ($2.60–4.25 at the parallel rate; $3.05–4.96 at the official rate).**
> **Derivation:** the sourced Baghdad cappuccino benchmark is 3,300 IQD across a broad restaurant sample. Specialty/branded operators (The Grinders, Espressolab, Agora, IN OFF) sit above the sample mean; the sourced blended-iced-drink price of ~4,900 IQD ($3.78) is the best direct proxy for a premium cold drink. An iced latte therefore lands between the cappuccino floor and the frappuccino ceiling. Confidence: **medium — this is my number, not a published one.** Verify against an actual Grinders or Espressolab menu before it goes in the deck.

> **ESTIMATE — scoop of ice cream in Baghdad: 1,500–3,000 IQD ($1.00–2.00).** Derivation: triangulated between the Coca-Cola 2L retail price (1,635 IQD), the cheeseburger price (2,400–2,900 IQD), and the general finding that Baghdad is the cheapest of 41 Western Asian cities for restaurant items. A premium/imported-format scoop (Morelli's Gelato) would sit at the top of or above that range. **No direct published price was found.** Confidence: **low.**

> **ESTIMATE — fresh juice in Baghdad: 2,000–4,000 IQD ($1.30–2.60).** Derivation: input costs are sourced — local oranges 1,200–1,250 IQD/kg, bananas 1,000–1,750 IQD/kg (Iraqi Ministry of Agriculture wholesale bulletins, 2026) — implying a raw-material cost of roughly 400–700 IQD per 300ml glass; standard Middle East juice-bar markups of 4–6× give the range shown. Confidence: **low-medium.**

**Pricing implication for SHABM:** if a standard Baghdad cappuccino is 3,300 IQD and a blended iced drink is ~4,900 IQD, then a **"-80" frozen-cup dirty latte at 7,500–9,000 IQD ($4.90–5.90 parallel)** is a ~1.5–1.8× premium to the top of the existing cold-drink market, and an **ice-block-vessel drink at 12,000–15,000 IQD ($7.85–9.80)** is a 2.5–3× premium. Both are defensible **only** on theatre/scarcity, not on beverage quality — which is exactly why the ice-cube-storefront brand asset matters. For reference, 15,000 IQD is roughly **6% of average per-capita monthly expenditure (248,600 IQD)** — that is a genuine special-occasion purchase in Baghdad, not an everyday one. Model the ice-block SKU at low volume and high margin; model the -80 latte as the everyday driver.

The **+152% year-on-year jump in 2024** is the eye-catching number and the one worth stress-testing before use.

## 3.6 Delivery infrastructure (a real demand channel)

Operating in Iraq: **Talabat** (Delivery Hero; 6M+ active customers, 65,000+ partners, 119,000 riders across its 7-country footprint), **Toters**, **Lezzoo** (Iraqi, founded Erbil 2018), plus aggressive entry by **Careem** and **Uber**. Competition has driven service quality up and pricing down.

**Strategic caveat for SHABM:** three of your five product lines — the frozen -80 cup, the carved ice block, and the live-poured rolled ice cream — **cannot survive a delivery journey in a 45°C Baghdad summer.** This is a dine-in / grab-and-consume-immediately business. That is a constraint on revenue mix, and an investor will ask about it. The answer is that it is also a *moat*: a concept that cannot be delivered cannot be commoditised by an aggregator, and it forces the footfall that makes the storefront a media asset.

> **Derivation:** June, July and August have mean *daily highs* of 42°C, 45°C and 45°C respectively — meaning essentially every day in those three months (92 days) exceeds 40°C. May's mean high of 37°C implies roughly the last 10–14 days of May clear 40°C; September's mean high of 41°C implies roughly 20–25 days clear it; early October contributes a further ~5–10. Total: 92 + 12 + 22 + 8 ≈ **134 days**, with a plausible band of 120–140. Cross-check: Weather Spark's 3.9-month (≈118-day) window of *average highs above 38.9°C* is consistent with a slightly narrower 40°C count. Confidence: **medium.** No published day-count for Baghdad was located.

> ★ **ESTIMATE — days above 45°C per year in Baghdad: 40–60.**
> **Derivation:** July and August both have mean daily highs of exactly ~45°C, so by definition roughly half the days in each month exceed it (≈31 days), plus the hottest ~10 days of June and ~5 days of September. Total ≈ 46 days, band 40–60. Anchor point: EUISS puts days at the much higher 48.9°C threshold at ~14/year today, which is consistent with ~46 days at the 45°C threshold. Confidence: **medium.**

**The seasonality slide writes itself:** Baghdad delivers ~4 months (late May–late September) of structurally guaranteed extreme-heat demand for frozen product, plus a 3–4 month window (December–March) where an outdoor 4°C night makes a hot barista drink the obvious purchase. The genuine revenue risk is the **shoulder seasons — April and October–November** — where neither proposition is compelling. Model those months at a discount and be explicit about it; an investor who has operated seasonal F&B will look for exactly that.

# 5. BAGHDAD COMMERCIAL / FOOTFALL DISTRICTS

## 5.1 District-by-district

**MANSOUR (المنصور)** — *Highest-prestige option.*
- Character: upper-class district containing malls, universities, parks. Described as "an avid shopping district that attracts those seeking luxury imported goods, modern marketplaces, restaurants, cafes and entertainment." Full-service: schools, medical centres, luxury shopping.
- Key artery: **14 Ramadan Street (شارع ١٤ رمضان)** — a principal Baghdad commercial spine within Mansour; hosts corporate offices (SalamAir opened its Baghdad office in the Al Asal Building here in March 2024), restaurants (Khan Mandi), and existing ice-cream retail (**ICE PACK Almansour** — note: a direct-adjacent competitor already on this street).

## 7.1 Electricity — the number one operating risk for a freezer-dependent business

| Official business grid tariff | ~**USD 0.046/kWh** | GlobalPetrolPrices, June 2025 |

| Summer 2026 outlook | Ghadan Foundation for Risk Management warned of a **severe electricity shortfall ahead of summer 2026** | Kurdistan24 / GFRM, 2026 |

**Why this is existential rather than annoying for SHABM specifically.** Every other café in Baghdad loses inventory measured in milk and pastries when the power drops. SHABM's inventory *is* the cold chain:
- An **ultra-low-temperature freezer at −80°C** draws heavy continuous load and has a long, energy-expensive pull-down cycle. It cannot be cycled on generator power intermittently without either destroying the compressor or losing the entire frozen-cup stock.
- **Carved clear ice blocks** represent days of accumulated freezing energy per unit — the most capital-intensive inventory per gram in the store.
- The **rolled-ice-cream cold pan** must hold roughly −25°C continuously during service.
- The **fruit-shaped moulded sorbets** are a finished frozen SKU with no shelf life outside the freezer.

At 8–12 grid hours per day, **12–16 hours of every single day must be covered by private generation**, all year, with peak load coinciding exactly with peak ambient temperature (45°C) and peak neighbourhood generator demand. This is not a contingency line — it is a core, continuous cost of goods.

> **ESTIMATE — SHABM monthly power cost, single Baghdad unit:** a store running a −80°C ULT freezer, a blast/storage freezer, an ice-block freezer, a cold pan, refrigeration, air conditioning against 45°C ambient, and lighting would plausibly need **40–70 amperes** of neighbourhood generator capacity, or a dedicated on-site generator. At the sourced $8.40/ampere/month that is **$336–588/month** on shared supply; at the summer operator rate of 25,000 IQD/ampere it is **$500–875/month**. A dedicated diesel generator with fuel would likely run **$800–1,500/month** in summer. **Confidence: low — this is engineering judgement on top of sourced per-ampere rates, not a quoted figure.** An Iraqi electrical contractor should size this properly, and the answer belongs in the deck, because it is the first question a knowledgeable investor will ask.

**The strategic reframe for the deck:** the electricity constraint is simultaneously SHABM's **largest cost risk and its widest moat**. A competitor cannot casually copy a −80°C product line, because doing so requires solving continuous ULT power in a city with 8–12 grid hours. Own that answer — redundant on-site generation, ULT units with sufficient thermal mass to ride through switchover, and a documented cold-chain SOP — and it becomes a barrier to entry rather than a footnote.

### Step 6 — Single-unit revenue anchor
- At **300 units/day** at an average ticket of **6,000 IQD**:
- → 1.8M IQD/day × 365 = **657 million IQD/year ≈ US$429,000/year** at the parallel rate
- Against my estimated rent band of $600–3,000/month and estimated power of $500–1,500/month, this supports a viable unit — **but the ticket and the daily-unit assumptions are the two most fragile numbers in the entire model** and both need Baghdad-specific validation before the raise.
